terms.meaning: A number that scientists work out for light, heat, movement and electricity. When things change, the total stays the same. Nobody can yet say what energy is, only how it behaves.
terms.example: Sunlight warms your hand. The light's energy turns into the hand's heat, and the two add up to the same total.
terms.art: Sunlight falling on a child's hand, with a small arrow from the light to the warm skin.

terms.meaning: Energy that moves from a hotter thing to a cooler thing.
terms.example: A steel tumbler of hot tea warms your hands, because heat flows from the tumbler into them.
terms.art: A child's two hands wrapped around a steaming steel tumbler, with small arrows going from the tumbler into the hands.

terms.meaning: A kind of light that our eyes cannot see. We feel it as warmth.
terms.example: Hold your hand beside a warm tava without touching it. The warmth you feel is infrared.
terms.art: A hand held beside a warm tava with wavy lines coming off the tava towards the hand.

terms.meaning: A measure of how fast energy arrives or is used.
terms.example: A small LED bulb uses about 10 watts. Noon sunlight brings about 1,000 watts to every square metre of ground.
terms.art: A small LED bulb marked 10 W beside a bright terrace square marked 1,000 W.

terms.meaning: The size of a square that is 1 metre long and 1 metre wide.
terms.example: Four floor tiles, each 50 centimetres wide, laid in a big square cover one square metre.
terms.art: Four floor tiles in a two-by-two square with a metre stick along each side.

terms.meaning: Water that has turned into a gas that mixes with the air. We cannot see it.
terms.example: Wet clothes on a line dry because their water slowly leaves as vapour.
terms.art: A wet cloth on a line in the sun with faint wavy arrows rising from it.

terms.meaning: To take in. A surface that absorbs light keeps its energy, and the energy turns into heat.
terms.example: Black tar absorbs most of the sunlight that falls on it, so it is too hot to walk on at noon.
terms.art: A black tar road and a white painted line, with thick arrows of sunlight going into the tar.

terms.meaning: To send light away again without keeping it.
terms.example: Kitchen foil reflects most of the sunlight that lands on it, so it stays cooler than black paper.
terms.art: A sheet of foil sending a sunbeam off at an angle on a sunny table.

terms.meaning: A number that says how hot or cold something is.
terms.example: Bath-warm water is about 40 degrees Celsius. Water boils at about 100 degrees Celsius.
terms.art: Three tumblers labelled cool, warm and hot with a number beside each.

terms.meaning: A tool that measures temperature.
terms.example: A kitchen thermometer dipped in a steel tumbler of tea shows how hot the tea is.
terms.art: A digital kitchen thermometer standing in a steel tumbler of water.

terms.meaning: A box that cooks food with sunlight. It has a black inside, a clear cover and a shiny flap.
terms.example: The box you build for the Sun Box test is a small solar box cooker.
terms.art: A cardboard box with a clear cover and a foil flap tilted towards the Sun.

terms.meaning: A material that heat passes through only slowly.
terms.example: A woollen sweater and a lunch bag lined with foam are insulators. They keep a warm thing warm for longer.
terms.art: A steel tiffin wrapped in a thick cloth with small arrows of heat trying to leave and slowing down.

terms.meaning: The one small place where a curved mirror brings light together.
terms.example: The pot of a dish cooker sits at the focus of its curved mirror, where the light of the whole dish gathers.
terms.art: A bowl-shaped mirror with rays of sunlight bending to meet at one point above it.

terms.meaning: A smooth curve, open on one side, like the path of a thrown ball. A mirror in this shape sends all straight rays to one point.
terms.example: A satellite television dish is a parabola. Its receiver sits at the focus.
terms.art: A parabola drawn on grid paper with parallel rays reflecting to a point.

terms.meaning: Water that has turned into a very hot gas, which forms when water boils.
terms.example: Steam rises from a rice pot and from idlis in a steamer.
terms.art: An idli steamer with a plume of steam rising from under the lid.

terms.meaning: A rooftop device that heats water with sunlight and keeps the hot water in a wrapped tank.
terms.example: Many homes in Bengaluru and Pune get their bathing water from a solar water heater on the roof.
terms.art: A slanted rooftop panel with glass tubes and a round tank across the top.

terms.meaning: Energy carried by tiny charged particles that move along a wire.
terms.example: The electricity that lights a bulb is a flow of tiny particles through the wire.
terms.art: A bulb joined by a wire to a battery, with small dots moving along the wire.

terms.meaning: A tiny charged particle found in every atom. Electrons moving along a wire are what we call electric current.
terms.example: In the wire of a lit bulb, billions upon billions of electrons are moving at the same time.
terms.art: An atom drawn as a ball with tiny dots around it, and an arrow pulling one dot out into a wire.

terms.meaning: A thin slice of material, usually silicon, that gives an electric current when light falls on it.
terms.example: The dark strip above the screen of a pocket calculator is a solar cell.
terms.art: A pocket calculator with a dark strip above its screen and light falling on the strip.

terms.meaning: A grey material made from quartz sand. It is used in solar cells and in computer chips.
terms.example: Most sand on the beach holds quartz, the mineral that silicon is made from.
terms.art: A handful of sand beside a shiny grey slice of silicon.

terms.meaning: Many solar cells joined side by side under a sheet of glass.
terms.example: Solar panels on the roof of Kochi airport in Kerala make electricity from sunlight all day.
terms.art: A rooftop panel made of rows of small dark squares under glass.

terms.meaning: A tiny packet of light energy. A beam of light is a stream of photons.
terms.example: When you switch on a torch, an enormous number of photons leave it every second.
terms.art: A torch beam drawn as a stream of tiny dots.

terms.meaning: The flow of electrons along a wire.
terms.example: A fan runs while current flows through its wire, and stops when you switch the current off.
terms.art: A wire with a row of dots moving along it and an arrow showing the direction.

terms.meaning: A container that stores electric energy to use later.
terms.example: A solar lantern's battery fills up by day and lights the lantern in the evening.
terms.art: A solar lantern with a small panel on top and a battery inside.

terms.meaning: A large area covered with solar panels that send electricity into the wires of a region.
terms.example: Bhadla Solar Park in the Thar desert of Rajasthan covers about 56 square kilometres.
terms.art: Rows and rows of solar panels on flat desert land under a bright sky.

terms.meaning: Sitting in the Sun to warm the body.
terms.example: A garden lizard basks on a wall in the morning and goes into the shade once warm enough.
terms.art: A garden lizard lying flat on a sunny wall.

terms.meaning: A tiny group of atoms joined together. Every kind of thing is made of molecules or atoms.
terms.example: One molecule of water has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom joined together.
terms.art: A water molecule drawn as one large ball with two small balls attached.

terms.meaning: The lightest kind of atom. The Sun is mostly hydrogen.
terms.example: Every drop of water has hydrogen in it, joined to oxygen.
terms.art: A water molecule drawn as one large ball with two small balls attached.

terms.meaning: The second lightest kind of atom. It is made when hydrogen joins together in the Sun's centre.
terms.example: Helium fills the balloons that float up at a fair, because it is lighter than air.
terms.art: A bunch of floating balloons held by a child at a fair.

terms.meaning: A very tiny particle made in the Sun's centre that passes through almost everything.
terms.example: About 6,000 crore neutrinos from the Sun pass through your fingernail every second, and you feel none of them.
terms.art: A fingernail with faint dotted lines passing straight through it.

terms.meaning: A time when the Moon or the Earth hides the Sun or the Moon from view.
terms.example: In a total solar eclipse, the Moon covers the whole of the Sun for a few minutes and the day goes dim.
terms.art: The Moon in front of the Sun with a ring of light around it.

terms.meaning: The Sun's outermost layer of thin, glowing gas. It is hotter than 10 lakh degrees Celsius.
terms.example: During a total solar eclipse, the corona shows as a pearly white halo around the dark Moon.
terms.art: A dark disc with a soft white halo of rays around it.

terms.meaning: A fuel such as coal, oil or gas that formed from the remains of living beings buried for millions of years.
terms.example: Cooking gas in a cylinder is a fossil fuel. It holds sunlight that plants caught long ago.
terms.art: A gas cylinder beside a plant with an arrow from the Sun to the plant.

terms.meaning: A kind of light that our eyes cannot see. It has more energy than violet light.
terms.example: Ultraviolet in sunlight tans and burns skin. It also helps to kill germs in clear water.
terms.art: A child under a cap on a sunny day with faint violet arrows coming from the Sun.

terms.meaning: A tiny green part inside a plant cell. It uses light to make sugar from air and water.
terms.example: The green of a leaf is the colour of the chloroplasts inside its cells.
terms.art: A cut leaf with one cell enlarged to show small green ovals inside.

terms.meaning: A coloured substance that absorbs some colours of light and reflects the rest.
terms.example: A green leaf reflects green light and absorbs mostly red and blue light. Its pigment is called chlorophyll.
terms.art: A green leaf with arrows of red and blue light going in and green light bouncing out.

experiments.title: The Sun Box test: does a box with a clear cover heat water more than the open Sun?
experiments.question: Two steel tumblers hold the same amount of water in the same sunlight for the same time. One stands in the open. The other stands in a black box with a clear cover and a foil flap. Which water ends up hotter, and why?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess which tumbler will be hotter after one hour in the Sun, and by how many degrees. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Both tumblers are the same size, hold 150 millilitres of the same tap water and wear the same black paper. They start at the same temperature. They stand side by side in the same sunlight for the same 60 minutes. The only thing that differs is the box with its clear cover and foil flap. The two tumblers are in the same sun at the same moment, so the Sun is the same for both. If you can, repeat the whole test on a second sunny day, because one day can be unusual.
results_table: Touch: cool, warm, hot or too hot
experiments.safety: Never look at the Sun, and never look at the bright spot that foil or a mirror throws. Check the aim only by looking at the box's shadow. The tumblers, the black paper and the clear cover get hot enough to burn, so an adult lifts them. Never use a plastic bottle as a lid over food.

materials.item: 2 identical steel tumblers or small steel bowls, 7 to 10 centimetres tall
a cardboard box about 30 centimetres long and 12 to 15 centimetres deep, taller than the tumblers, such as a shoebox
matt black paper or black chart paper, 4 sheets
a clear plastic sheet or the glass of an old photo frame, 2 centimetres larger than the box opening all round
spare card for the flap, the size of the box opening
aluminium foil, enough to cover the flap
clear tape and a glue stick
a ruler or a stick to prop the flap
a kitchen thermometer that reads above 80 degrees Celsius (or use the touch test)
a measuring jug or a cup marked in millilitres, and a jug of tap water
a folded newspaper for the open tumbler to stand on
a phone or watch, a pencil and paper

experiments.record: Fill in the table: start and end temperature for each tumbler, and the rise. Draw the two rises as two bars on a strip of paper, one beside the other. Then write one sentence each for what I think, what I saw and why. Add one sentence on what this test cannot tell us.
experiments.context: In the Sun Box test you put two tumblers of water in the same sunlight. One stands in the open and one in a box you make. You find out whether a box that adds no heat can still make the water hotter.

setup.art: A shoebox lined with black paper, with a clear sheet taped over its opening and a foil-covered flap standing up at the back edge.
setup.caption: 1. The box: black inside, a clear cover taped down and a foil flap at the back.

setup.art: Two steel tumblers wrapped in the same black paper, each with a thermometer in it, one on a table and one inside the box.
setup.caption: 2. Two matching tumblers with the same water at the same start temperature.

setup.art: A terrace floor in sunlight, the box facing the Sun with its shadow lying straight behind it, and the second tumbler on folded newspaper beside it.
setup.caption: 3. In the Sun. The box shadow falls straight behind the box. The open tumbler stands beside it.

setup.art: Two bars on a strip of paper, a short one labelled open and a tall one labelled box.
setup.caption: 4. After 60 minutes, draw how much each tumbler rose.

flow.do: Choose a day with direct sun for the next hour, between 10.30 in the morning and 2.30 in the afternoon. A balcony, a terrace or a sunny window sill all work. Choose the spot now and check that no shadow will cross it.
flow.say: We need one hour of real sunshine on a spot. Where in our home does the sun fall straight on the floor at midday?
flow.kid: Find a spot where the Sun shines straight in for the next hour.
flow.parent: If the sky is cloudy, or no direct sun reaches your home, do not run the test today. Build the box, and do the other parts of this lesson. Run the test on the next sunny day. Winter in the north has a low sun, so prop the back of the box up with a book to face the Sun. With no direct sun for days, a desk lamp with an old-style filament bulb of 60 to 100 watts works for a weaker version. Put the bulb 20 centimetres above the tumblers and the box. Keep it away from paper, and stay in the room for the 45 minutes. The rise is then only a few degrees, so use a thermometer.

flow.do: An adult cuts the pieces. Cut a clear sheet 2 centimetres bigger than the box opening on every side. Cut a card flap the same size as the opening. Cut black paper to cover the floor and four walls inside the box, and two pieces to wrap the tumblers.
flow.say: I will do all the cutting. After this you only glue and tape.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut the card, the clear sheet and the black paper.
flow.parent: Any of these works as a clear cover. Use a clear sheet from a stationery shop, a clear sweet-box lid or the glass of an old photo frame. If you use glass, tape every edge with two layers of tape. Never use a plastic bottle as a lid over food. Use matt black paper, because shiny black reflects a little light.

flow.do: Glue black paper to the floor and the four inside walls of the box. Wrap one piece of black paper round each tumbler from base to rim and tape it. Leave the top of each tumbler open.
flow.say: Both tumblers wear the same black paper. Why do you think we dress both of them the same way?
flow.kid: Line the box with black paper. Wrap both tumblers in black paper.
flow.parent: Both tumblers must be dressed the same, so the only difference is the box. A bare steel tumbler is shiny and would reflect much of the light, which would spoil the test.

flow.do: Glue foil to the card flap, shiny side out, as smooth as you can. Tape one long edge of the flap to the back edge of the box. The back is the edge that will face away from the Sun. Stand the flap up and lean it back a little. Use the ruler to prop it open.
flow.say: The foil is shiny. What do you think shiny foil will do to the sunlight that falls on it?
flow.kid: Glue foil on the flap. Tape the flap to the back of the box. Prop it open.
flow.parent: The flap leans back, away from the Sun, so its shiny face looks at the Sun and sends light down into the box.

flow.do: Pour 150 millilitres of tap water into each tumbler. Put a thermometer in each and write the two temperatures. They should match within one degree. If they do not, pour both from the same jug again.
flow.say: Why must both tumblers start with the same amount of water at the same temperature?
flow.kid: Pour the same amount of water into both tumblers. Read each temperature and write it down.
flow.parent: Without a thermometer, use the touch test in the reading step, and write cool, warm or hot for each tumbler now. Pour the water after the black paper is on, so a leak does not spoil the paper.

flow.do: Ask for the guess and the reason. Write both at the top of the page before anything goes into the Sun.
flow.say: Which tumbler will be hotter after an hour in the Sun? By how many degrees? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which tumbler will be hotter. Write your guess and your reason.

ask.q: Where could the extra heat in the box come from, if there is no flame and no wire?
good: The box holds the Sun's heat in.
The foil sends more light in.
The black paper takes in light and turns it into heat.
I do not know, so we test it.

flow.parent: Do not say who is right. The tumblers will answer. A child who says the box makes heat has an idea that the test can check.

flow.do: Take everything outside. Put the box in the Sun, with the foil flap on the side away from the Sun. Turn the box until its shadow lies straight behind it. Put one tumbler in the middle of the box. Tape the clear sheet down on all four sides, so no air can leak out.
flow.say: The box's shadow tells us where the Sun is. When the shadow lies straight behind the box, the Sun is shining straight in.
flow.kid: Turn the box until its shadow lies straight behind it. Put a tumbler in. Tape the cover down.
flow.parent: Check the aim only by the shadow. Do not look at the Sun or at the bright patch from the foil. Tilt the flap until a soft bright patch lies across the clear sheet.

flow.do: Put the second tumbler on a folded newspaper beside the box, in full sun and out of the box's shadow. Write down the time.
flow.say: The open tumbler gets the same sunlight as the one in the box. What do you think will be different?
flow.kid: Put the other tumbler beside the box on a folded newspaper. Write the time.
flow.wait: Leave both tumblers in the Sun for 60 minutes

flow.do: After 30 minutes, look at the box's shadow. If it no longer lies straight behind the box, turn the box until it does. Do not lift the cover.
flow.say: The Sun has moved a little. Why do we turn the box?
flow.kid: Check the shadow at 30 minutes. Turn the box if it needs it.
flow.parent: The Sun moves across the sky, about the width of a fist at arm's length in an hour. Lifting the cover now would let the warm air out and spoil the test.

flow.do: After 60 minutes, an adult lifts the clear sheet and reads the box tumbler first, within ten seconds. Then read the open tumbler. Write both temperatures. With no thermometer, the adult dips one fingertip into each tumbler for one second. The adult says cool, warm, hot or too hot.
flow.say: The box tumbler goes first. Why do you think we read it quickly?
flow.kid: A grown-up lifts the cover and reads the thermometers. Write both numbers.
flow.parent: On a clear summer noon, expect about 40 to 48 degrees Celsius for the open tumbler. Expect about 50 to 75 for the box tumbler. On a hazy day or in winter, expect about 30 to 38 and 40 to 55. Either way, the box tumbler should be at least 8 degrees ahead. If it is not, check that the clear sheet is sealed, the box was not in shade and the black paper is matt. A home box seldom passes 80 degrees, so do not promise cooked food. Never let a child put a finger into water the adult could not keep a finger in for three seconds. Pour the water on a plant when it is cool.

flow.do: Work out the rise in each tumbler, which is the end temperature minus the start. Draw the two rises as bars. Then say or write what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.say: Which tumbler rose more, and by how many degrees? The box added no heat. So why is the water hotter?
flow.kid: Work out each rise. Draw two bars. Write what you saw and why.

ask.q: What could you test next to find which part of the box matters most?
good: Take away one part at a time and test again.
Make two boxes, one without the clear cover.
Change only one thing in each test.

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. Ask the child to say why first. The explanation cards after this test show what the box is doing. The test cannot tell us which part did the most. The cover, the black paper and the foil all changed at once. It also cannot tell us what the water would do on a cloudy day.
flow.think: If the box adds no heat, what must it be doing to the heat that the Sun brings in?

experiments.title: Where does warm water go? Coloured water in cold and in hand-hot water
experiments.question: A solar water heater has its tank above its tubes. Does warm water rise above cold water, and does cold water sink below warm water?
experiments.predict: Before you pour, guess where the red warm water will go in the cold water. Then guess where the blue cold water will go in the warm water. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Both tumblers hold the same amount of water. Each coloured pour has the same drops of colour and the same amount of water. Each is poured slowly down the back of a spoon. The only thing that changes is the temperature of the water you pour. If a pour splashes and mixes, empty the tumbler and do it again, slower.
experiments.safety: Use only hand-hot water from the geyser tap, never water from a kettle or a pan. An adult tests it first with a fingertip, and pours it.

materials.item: 2 clear plastic tumblers or clear plastic jars
fridge-cold water, about 600 millilitres in all
hand-hot water from the geyser tap, about 300 millilitres
food colour in two colours, or two colours of washable ink
2 small cups and a teaspoon
a tablespoon
a steel tray to catch spills, and a cloth

experiments.record: Draw each tumbler after the pour with the coloured water in the place you saw it. Write one sentence each for what I think, what I saw and why. Say what this test cannot tell us about a real solar water heater.
experiments.context: In this experiment you pour red warm water onto cold water. You also pour blue cold water into warm water. You find out whether warm water rises and cold water sinks. A solar water heater uses this to move its water without a pump.
