setup.art: Two tumblers side by side, one with a red layer floating on top and one with a blue ribbon sinking to the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Look at where each colour goes.

flow.do: An adult runs the geyser tap until the water is hand-hot. That is warm enough that a fingertip stays in for 5 seconds without pain. Pour 200 millilitres into tumbler B. Pour 4 tablespoons into small cup 1. Put 200 millilitres of fridge-cold water into tumbler A, and 4 tablespoons into small cup 2.
flow.say: We need two temperatures. The tap gives hand-hot water and the fridge gives cold water. Which do you think is lighter?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up for hand-hot water. Set out the tumblers and cups.
flow.parent: Never use kettle water. If your home has no geyser, an adult warms water in a steel pan and lets it cool until hand-hot. The adult carries it in a jug. In winter, tap water may be cold enough for tumbler A without the fridge. For a stronger effect, add two ice cubes to the cold water for three minutes and take them out before the pour.

flow.do: Add 4 drops of red colour to cup 1, the warm cup. Add 4 drops of blue colour to cup 2, the cold cup. Stir each with a clean teaspoon.
flow.say: The red water is warm and the blue water is cold. Where will each one go?
flow.kid: Put red colour in the warm cup. Put blue colour in the cold cup.

flow.do: Ask for the guess and the reason about each pour. Write both down before you pour.
flow.say: Where will the red warm water go in the cold tumbler? Where will the blue cold water go in the warm tumbler? Why?
flow.kid: Guess where each colour will go. Write your reason.

ask.q: Where do you think the warm red water will settle in the cold tumbler?
good: On top, because warm water is lighter.
At the bottom, because heat sinks.
It will mix straight away.

flow.parent: Do not say who is right. The tumblers will show.

flow.do: Hold a tablespoon against the inside wall of tumbler A, with its back just above the water. Pour the red warm water slowly onto the back of the spoon. Watch for one minute without touching the tumbler.
flow.say: Pour slowly so the water settles. What is the red water doing?
flow.kid: Pour the red water slowly down the back of the spoon. Watch it.
flow.parent: Expect a red layer that floats on top of the cold water and stays as a separate layer for a minute or two. If it mixes at once, the pour was too fast or the water was not warm enough. Empty the tumbler and pour again.

flow.do: Hold the spoon the same way against the wall of tumbler B, the hand-hot one. Pour the blue cold water slowly onto the spoon. Watch for one minute.
flow.say: Now the blue water is the cold one. What is it doing?
flow.kid: Pour the blue water slowly down the back of the spoon. Watch it.
flow.parent: Expect a blue ribbon that slides down to the bottom within a few seconds. In winter, if the blue water is not much colder than the tumbler, the ribbon is slower and fainter. Use the ice trick from the first step.

flow.do: Watch both tumblers for 5 minutes. Draw where the colours are at the start and at the end. The layers slowly mix as heat moves from warm water to cold water.
flow.say: What happens to the colours after 5 minutes? Why do you think the layers fade?
flow.kid: Draw both tumblers now and again after 5 minutes.

ask.q: In a solar water heater, which water do you want in the tank at the top?
good: The warm water, because it rises there by itself.
The hot water, so it can be stored and kept warm.

flow.parent: The layers fade because heat passes slowly from the warm water into the cold water, and the water then moves and mixes. This test cannot show the whole loop of a real heater, only that warm water goes up and cold water goes down.

flow.do: Say or write what you think, what you saw and why. Pour the coloured water onto a plant and wash the tumblers.
flow.say: Why is the tank of a solar water heater always above its tubes?
flow.kid: Say what you saw and why. Then wash up.
flow.think: Could a hose of warm water run downhill by itself, and what would be needed to push it up?

activities.title: Black, white or foil: which sheet feels warmest after ten minutes in the Sun?
activities.context: In this activity you lay a black sheet, a white sheet and a sheet of foil in the same sunlight. You feel which is warmest. You find out which surfaces absorb light and which reflect it.
activities.safety: Never look at the Sun or at the bright spot that foil throws.

materials.item: a sheet of black chart paper
a sheet of white paper of the same size
a sheet of aluminium foil of the same size, shiny side up
a flat board or tray to lay them on
4 coins to hold the corners down
a kitchen thermometer (optional)

schedule.what: Guess, lay out the three sheets in the Sun for 10 minutes, feel them and rank them.

activities.record: Draw the three sheets in a row. Shade each one from cool to warm. Write one sentence on which absorbed the most light and how you know.

setup.art: A black sheet, a white sheet and a foil sheet side by side on a flat board with a coin on every corner.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the three sheets side by side on one board, with a coin on each corner.

setup.art: The board on a sunny balcony floor, with a child's back of the hand held just above each sheet.
setup.caption: 2. After ten minutes, feel each sheet with the back of your hand.

setup.art: Three sheets in a row labelled coolest, middle and warmest.
setup.caption: 3. Put the three sheets in order from coolest to warmest.

flow.do: Lay the three sheets side by side on one board, in the same sunny spot. Put a coin on every corner so the wind cannot lift them. Keep the shiny side of the foil facing up.
flow.say: These three sheets get the same sunlight. Which one do you think will feel warmest after ten minutes? Why?
flow.kid: Lay the black, white and foil sheets side by side. Put a coin on each corner.
flow.parent: Choose a spot with direct sun. If the sky is cloudy, the sheets will feel nearly the same. Try again on a sunny day. Or use a desk lamp with an old-style bulb of 60 to 100 watts, held 15 centimetres above the sheets for ten minutes. Never leave a lamp alone.

flow.do: Ask for the guess and the reason. Write both before the sheets go into the Sun.
flow.say: Which sheet will feel warmest, and which coolest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess the warmest sheet. Write your reason.

ask.q: What do you think the foil will do to the sunlight?
good: Send it away, so it stays cooler.
Bounce it off like a mirror.
Take it in, like the black one.

flow.parent: Do not say who is right. Let the sheets answer.

flow.do: Leave the sheets in the Sun for ten minutes. Do not touch them. Look at them again at five minutes, to see if anything has changed.
flow.say: While we wait, the sunlight is arriving on all three sheets. What do you think happens to the light that lands on the black one?
flow.kid: Leave the sheets for ten minutes. Do not touch them.
flow.wait: Leave the sheets in the Sun for 10 minutes

flow.do: Feel each sheet with the back of your hand for two seconds. Put them in order from coolest to warmest. With a thermometer, lay it on each sheet in turn. Cover it with a folded cloth for a minute, then read it.
flow.say: Which one is warmest? Which is coolest? Does that match your guess?
flow.kid: Touch each sheet with the back of your hand. Put them in order.

ask.q: Why is the black sheet warmer than the white one in the same sunlight?
good: Black takes in more of the light and turns it into heat.
White sends more of the light away.

flow.parent: Expect the black sheet to be clearly warmest. White and foil should feel cooler. Foil can feel warm too, because metal passes heat quickly, but it takes in little light.

flow.do: Say or write what you think, what you saw and why. Put the sheets away.
flow.say: Where else have you seen black things get hotter than white things in the Sun?
flow.kid: Say what you saw and why.
flow.think: Which colour would you paint the roof of a house in your town, and why?

activities.title: Sun detectives: five jobs the Sun does in your home and street today
activities.context: In this activity you look for the jobs sunlight is doing around you, such as drying, warming and lighting. You find out how many ways your family already uses the Sun without a machine.

materials.item: a pencil and paper
a clock or a phone

schedule.what: Look for five jobs the Sun does, and draw where its patch of light lands in one room.

activities.record: Write five jobs the Sun is doing today, with the place where you saw each one. Draw a plan of one room from above, and shade where the Sun lands at two different times.

setup.art: A child with a pencil and a clipboard looking at a clothes line, a window and a rooftop with a solar water heater.
setup.caption: 1. Walk through your home and look out of the windows for Sun jobs.

setup.art: A plan of a room drawn from above with a patch of sunlight shaded in two different places.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the room from above and shade where the Sun lands.

flow.do: Look for these seven signs of the Sun at work. Wet clothes drying. Pickles or vadam drying. Light from a window. A warm patch on the floor. A solar water heater on a roof. An animal sitting in the Sun. A plant leaning towards a window.
flow.say: The Sun may be doing a job in your home right now. Where would you look first?
flow.kid: Read the list. Choose where to look first.
flow.parent: In a flat with no balcony, look out of the window at roofs, clothes lines and street animals. Do this in daylight on any day, sunny or not.

flow.do: Walk through your home, your balcony or your lane. Write each Sun job you find and the place. Find five. Count a window letting in light as one.
flow.say: Is the Sun doing this job with a machine or without one?
flow.kid: Find five jobs the Sun is doing. Write where.

ask.q: Which job would stop first if the Sun disappeared tomorrow?
good: Drying, because nothing would give the water energy to leave.
Daylight in the room.
Everything, because plants and food depend on it.

flow.parent: A cloudy day still gives daylight, so the window counts. On a cloudy day, drying is slower. Ask your child what difference that makes.

flow.do: Pick one room with a sunny patch. Draw the room from above. Shade where the Sun lands now and write the time. Come back two hours later or the same time the next day and shade the second patch.
flow.say: The Sun has moved. How do you know it moved, when you cannot see it move?
flow.kid: Draw one room from above. Shade the sunny patch and write the time.
flow.parent: The patch moves because the Earth turns. It moves about the width of a hand each hour on most floors.

flow.do: Look at your five jobs. Mark each job S if sunlight does it directly. Mark it M if a machine, such as a solar panel or a solar heater, first turns the sunlight into something else.
flow.say: Which jobs were done by sunlight itself and which needed a machine?
flow.kid: Mark each job S or M.
flow.think: What job could the Sun do that nobody in your family uses it for yet?

activities.title: The drying race: a wet cloth in the Sun and a wet cloth in the shade
activities.context: In this activity you hang two equally wet cloths, one in the Sun and one in the shade, and see which dries first. You find out what sunlight gives to water that makes the water leave as vapour.

materials.item: 2 identical small cloths, such as handkerchiefs
a bowl of water
2 clothes pegs or clips
a clothes line or a string
a clock or a phone

schedule.what: Wet two cloths equally, hang one in the Sun and one in the shade, and check every ten minutes.

activities.record: Write what each cloth felt like at 10, 20, 30 and 40 minutes: wet, damp or dry. Write which dried first and by about how many minutes.

setup.art: Two identical cloths held under the same tap and wrung out by the same number of squeezes.
setup.caption: 1. Wet both cloths in the same bowl and wring each one the same way.

setup.art: One cloth pegged on a line in sunlight and the other on a line in the shade of a wall, at the same height.
setup.caption: 2. Hang one in the Sun and one in the shade at the same height.

setup.art: A child pressing a cloth with a fingertip to feel if it is wet, damp or dry.
setup.caption: 3. Every ten minutes, press each cloth with a fingertip.

flow.do: Soak both cloths in the same bowl of water. Wring each one the same way, with ten firm twists. This makes them equally wet.
flow.say: We want both cloths wet in the same way. Why does that matter?
flow.kid: Wet both cloths. Wring each one ten times.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason. Then hang one cloth in the Sun and the other in the shade of a wall. Hang them at the same height, in the same breeze if you can.
flow.say: Which cloth will dry first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which cloth dries first. Hang one in the Sun and one in the shade.

ask.q: What gives the water in the cloth the energy to leave?
good: Heat from the Sun.
Warm air.
The sunlight turns into heat in the cloth and the water.

flow.parent: Keep the two places as alike as you can except for the Sun. A windy spot dries the cloth faster, so use two spots with about the same breeze. In a humid monsoon week both cloths dry slowly. Give the race an hour, or use a sunny window and a shady corner of the same room.

flow.do: Every ten minutes, press each cloth with a fingertip and write wet, damp or dry. Do not squeeze them. Stop when one is dry.
flow.say: Which cloth is drier now? What is happening to the water that was in it?
flow.kid: Press each cloth every ten minutes. Write wet, damp or dry.
flow.parent: The water has not vanished. It has left as vapour, mixed into the air.

flow.do: Say or write what you think, what you saw and why. Mention the word vapour. Take the cloths in.
flow.say: Where did the water in the cloth go? What did the Sun give it?
flow.kid: Say where the water went and why the Sun cloth dried first.
flow.think: Why do people dry vadam and fish in the Sun and not in the shade?

activities.title: Cover the solar cell: how much light does a solar calculator need?
activities.context: In this activity you cover a solar cell a little at a time and watch what happens to the thing it runs. You find out that a solar cell gives less electricity when less light reaches it.

materials.item: a pocket calculator with no battery, or a solar toy, a solar garden light or a small solar fan
a sheet of card or a strip of thick paper
a torch or a desk lamp

schedule.what: Run a solar calculator or toy in light. Cover one quarter, one half and all of its cell, and write what happens.

activities.record: Draw the cell with the covered part shaded for each test. Write beside each drawing what happened to the numbers or the movement.

setup.art: A pocket calculator with a dark strip above its screen held near a window.
setup.caption: 1. Switch on the calculator in good light and type some numbers.

setup.art: The same calculator with half of the dark strip hidden under a card.
setup.caption: 2. Cover half of the solar strip with a card.

setup.art: The calculator with the whole strip covered and a blank screen.
setup.caption: 3. Cover the whole strip.

flow.do: Find out if your calculator runs on light. Look for the word solar and for no battery cover on the back. Take it to a window or switch on a lamp over it. Press the keys and check the numbers show.
flow.say: Some calculators run on the dark strip above the screen. What do you think that strip is?
flow.kid: Take the solar calculator to the light. Press some keys.
flow.parent: A calculator with the word solar and no battery door runs on light alone. If yours has a battery, the numbers will not fade. Use a solar toy, a solar garden light or a small solar kit instead. In dim light, a bright torch held 10 centimetres from the cell works.

flow.do: Ask for a guess. Cover about a quarter of the strip with a card. Then about half. Then all of it. Look at the numbers each time.
flow.say: What do you think will happen to the numbers when you cover half of the strip?
flow.kid: Guess what happens. Cover a quarter, then half, then all of the strip.

ask.q: Why does a calculator work in dim light but a fan does not?
good: The calculator needs very little electricity.
A fan needs much more electricity, so more light.

flow.parent: Many calculators keep working with half the cell covered, because they need little electricity. A solar toy with a motor slows down at once. Both show that less light gives less electricity.

flow.do: Try three tests. Cover a quarter, then half, then all of the strip. Wait two seconds each time and watch. Write what you see in your record.
flow.say: What happens when you move the card away again?
flow.kid: Cover and uncover the strip. Watch the numbers.

flow.do: Say or write what you saw and why. A solar cell gives electricity only while light lands on it. Put the calculator away.
flow.say: Why would a solar lantern shine for fewer hours after a cloudy day?
flow.kid: Say what you saw and why.
flow.think: Is a photon like a tiny worker, and how many do you think the cell needs?

activities.title: Fold a parabola: draw the curve of a dish cooker's mirror
activities.context: In this activity you fold paper again and again to draw a curve called a parabola. You find out why a mirror in this shape sends sunlight to one place, as in a dish cooker.

materials.item: a sheet of thin paper, such as tracing paper, baking paper or photocopy paper
a ruler and a pencil
a coloured pen

schedule.what: Fold a line onto a dot about 25 times, and look at the curve the folds make.

activities.record: Keep the folded sheet. Draw the two lines for three ticks, and write their lengths. Write one sentence on why the dot is the best place for a cooking pot.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a line drawn along the bottom and a dot about 3 centimetres above the line, near the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a line along the bottom and a dot above it.

setup.art: A hand folding the paper so that one point of the line lands exactly on the dot, then creasing it.
setup.caption: 2. Fold a point on the line onto the dot and crease it.

setup.art: An open sheet covered with creases that together outline a smooth curve above the dot.
setup.caption: 3. Open the sheet. The creases outline a curve.

flow.do: Draw a straight line along the bottom of the sheet, about 2 centimetres from the edge. Draw a dot about 3 centimetres above the middle of the line. Mark small ticks on the line, 1 centimetre apart.
flow.say: The dot is where a cooking pot will sit. The line stands for the sunlight coming straight down. Why would a pot go at the dot?
flow.kid: Draw a line near the bottom. Draw a dot above it. Mark ticks along the line.

flow.do: Fold the paper so that the first tick on the line lands exactly on the dot. Press the crease flat. Open the paper. Do the same with every tick along the line. Make about 25 creases.
flow.say: Each crease is one tiny flat mirror. Which way does each one tilt?
flow.kid: Fold each tick onto the dot. Crease it. Do about 25.
flow.parent: Thin paper shows the creases best. Use a coloured pen to go over each crease if they are faint. Fold exactly onto the dot, because a crease that misses the dot spoils the curve.

flow.do: Open the sheet. The creases outline a smooth curve above the dot. Pick three ticks. From each tick, draw a straight line up, at a right angle to the bottom line. Stop where it meets the crease made from that tick. Then draw a line from that point to the dot.
flow.say: Sunlight comes straight down and hits the crease at that point. Where does the crease send it? Measure the two lines. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Pick a tick. Draw a line straight up to its crease. Then draw on to the dot.
flow.parent: Each crease cuts the line from a tick to the dot exactly in half, at a right angle. So the two lines you draw are equal in length. A ray from above that hits the crease at that point is sent on to the dot. That is how every dish cooker works. A mirror cut to this curve sends all straight rays to one point.

flow.do: Say or write what you saw and why. A dish cooker's mirror is this curve turned into a bowl. The pot sits at the dot, the focus.
flow.say: Why does the pot sit at the dot and not anywhere else in the bowl?
flow.kid: Say what the curve does to sunlight.
flow.think: If the Sun moves, what must a dish cooker do to keep the light at the dot?

projects.title: One part at a time: which job of the Sun Box matters most?
projects.context: In this project you build a second box and change one part of it each sunny day. You find out which job matters most: the clear cover, the black lining, the foil flap or the packing.
projects.safety: Never look at the Sun, and never look at the bright spot that foil or a mirror throws. Check the aim only by looking at the box's shadow. The tumblers, the black paper and the clear cover get hot enough to burn, so an adult lifts them. Never use a plastic bottle as a lid over food.

materials.item: the Sun Box and its tumbler from the Sun Box test
a second box of the same size, with a clear sheet, black paper and a foil flap
2 identical steel tumblers wrapped in the same black paper
white paper, for one day's test
newspaper, 6 sheets
a kitchen thermometer that reads above 80 degrees Celsius
clear tape, glue and a ruler
a pencil, a ruler and squared paper for the graph

schedule.what: Build the second box, which we call B. Run both boxes together to check they are twins.
Take the clear cover off box B. Run both boxes for 60 minutes. Compare.
Put the cover back. Change the lining of box B to white paper. Run both boxes. Compare.
Put the black lining back. Take the foil flap off box B. Run both. Compare.
Put the flap back. Pack crumpled newspaper around box B's tumbler. Run both. Then draw the graph and rank the parts.

projects.record: Keep a table with one row for each day. Write the rise in box A, the rise in box B, and the difference. Draw a bar graph of the four differences. Then put the four parts in order from the one that matters most to the one that matters least.

setup.art: Two matching boxes side by side on a terrace floor, each with a black lining, a clear cover and a foil flap, and a thermometer beside each.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: two matching boxes, A and B, run side by side.

setup.art: Box B with its clear cover removed, beside box A with its cover on.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: take the clear cover off box B.

setup.art: Box B lined with white paper beside box A lined with black paper.
setup.caption: 3. Day 3: line box B with white paper.

setup.art: Box B with no foil flap beside box A with its flap up.
setup.caption: 4. Day 4: take the foil flap off box B.

setup.art: A bar graph with four bars labelled cover, black lining, foil flap and packing.
setup.caption: 5. Day 5: draw the graph and put the parts in order.

flow.do: Build box B the same size as box A and in the same way. Put black paper inside, tape a clear sheet over the opening and add a foil flap at the back. Wrap a second tumbler in the same black paper. Cutting is for an adult.
flow.say: Box B must be a twin of box A. Why do we need twins before we change anything?
flow.kid: Build a second box like the first one. Wrap a second tumbler.
flow.parent: Build it on a day when you cannot run the test, so every sunny day goes to testing. A cloudy day is never lost: skip it and run that day's test on the next sunny day.

flow.do: Pour 150 millilitres of the same tap water into both tumblers. Read both temperatures. Put one tumbler in each box. Tape the covers down. Stand both boxes side by side in the same sunny spot, with their shadows straight behind them. Write the time. Leave them for 60 minutes.
flow.say: Both boxes are the same now. What do you think the two temperatures will be after an hour?
flow.kid: Put a tumbler in each box. Set both in the Sun. Write the time.
flow.parent: Start between 10.30 in the morning and 12.30 in the afternoon, so the Sun stays strong for the hour. Check the shadow at 30 minutes. If the day is cloudy, do not run the test today.
flow.wait: Leave both boxes in the Sun for 60 minutes

flow.do: An adult lifts each cover for a few seconds and reads each tumbler. Write both temperatures and the rise. The two boxes should be within 3 degrees of each other. If they are not, find out why, for example a leaking cover or a shadow.
flow.say: Are the twins really twins? What would you check if they were not?
flow.kid: A grown-up reads both. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: If one box is 3 or more degrees behind, look at the seal, the black paper and the shade. Fix it and repeat day 1. Never put a finger in the water unless an adult has tested it.

flow.do: Day 2. Take the clear cover off box B. Pour fresh tap water into both tumblers and read the starts. Put both boxes side by side in the Sun for 60 minutes, as on day 1.
flow.say: Box B has lost its clear cover. How many degrees do you think it will lose compared with box A?
flow.kid: Take the cover off box B. Set both in the Sun.
flow.wait: Leave both boxes in the Sun for 60 minutes

flow.do: An adult reads both tumblers. Write the rises and the difference between box A and box B.
flow.say: What has the clear cover been doing for box A?
flow.kid: A grown-up reads both. Write the difference.
flow.parent: Expect box B to lose many degrees. A clear cover mostly stops the warm air leaving, as Robert Wood found in 1909. If the difference is small on a windless day, repeat when there is a breeze.

flow.do: Day 3. Put the cover back on box B. Replace its black lining with white paper, and wrap its tumbler in black as before. Run both boxes for 60 minutes with fresh water.
flow.say: Now only the colour of the lining is different. What will the white lining do to the light?
flow.kid: Put the cover back. Line box B with white paper. Set both in the Sun.
flow.wait: Leave both boxes in the Sun for 60 minutes

flow.do: An adult reads both tumblers. Write the rises and the difference.
flow.say: Which cost box B more heat: no cover or white paper?
flow.kid: A grown-up reads both. Write the difference.

flow.do: Day 4. Put the black lining back in box B. Take its foil flap off. Run both boxes for 60 minutes with fresh water.
flow.say: Without the flap, less light reaches the tumbler. How many degrees will that cost?
flow.kid: Put black paper back in box B. Take the flap off. Set both in the Sun.
flow.wait: Leave both boxes in the Sun for 60 minutes

flow.do: An adult reads both tumblers. Write the rises and the difference.
flow.say: Was the flap worth more or less than the cover?
flow.kid: A grown-up reads both. Write the difference.

flow.do: Day 5. Put the foil flap back on box B. Pack crumpled newspaper between the tumbler and the box walls in box B. Run both boxes for 60 minutes with fresh water.
flow.say: The newspaper is an insulator. What do you think it will do?
flow.kid: Pack newspaper around the tumbler in box B. Set both in the Sun.
flow.parent: Keep the clear cover on and make sure no paper touches the cover or covers the tumbler's top.
flow.wait: Leave both boxes in the Sun for 60 minutes

flow.do: An adult reads both tumblers. Write the rises and the difference. This time box B may be hotter than box A.
flow.say: Did the extra packing help, hurt or do nothing?
flow.kid: A grown-up reads both. Write the difference.

flow.do: Draw a bar graph of the four differences on squared paper. Put the four parts in order from the one that mattered most to the one that mattered least. Write what the test cannot tell us.
flow.say: Which job mattered most: keeping heat in, or bringing more light in? Does that match your guess?
flow.kid: Draw the graph. Put the four parts in order.
flow.parent: The size of each loss depends on the day, so the order may change on a windy day or a hazy one. Repeat the part that surprised you before you trust it. This test cannot tell us how the parts work together, because each day removes only one.
flow.think: If a box could have just one of these four parts, which would you keep?

challenges.title: Keep the heat in: keep a tumbler of warm water warm for two hours
challenges.context: This is a design problem. A solar cooker is good at catching heat and poor at keeping it. You design a way to slow the heat's leaving from a tumbler of warm water.
challenges.problem: Keep 200 millilitres of hand-hot water in a steel tumbler as warm as possible for two hours. Use only things at home, with no flame, no heater and no electricity. A plain tumbler left on the table is your comparison. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Every design starts with the same amount of water at the same temperature, poured from the same jug.
Use only things you already have at home, such as cloth, paper, card, bubble wrap, old clothes or a basket.
Measure the temperature at the start, after 1 hour and after 2 hours. Do not open a design more often than that, because opening lets heat out.
This is water only. Food kept warm for hours should stay above about 60 degrees Celsius to be safe to eat. Never turn a design like this into a food keeper without a thermometer.
challenges.safety: Use only hand-hot water from the geyser tap. An adult tests it with a fingertip and pours it.

materials.item: 3 or more identical steel tumblers
a kitchen thermometer
a thick towel, an old woollen sweater or a cushion
newspaper, a cardboard box and a basket or a bucket
bubble wrap, aluminium foil, dry rice, straw or old cloth
a phone or a watch
paper and a pencil for the table

setup.art: Three steel tumblers on a tray: one bare, one wrapped in a thick towel and one inside a cardboard box packed with crumpled newspaper.
setup.caption: 1. Make two or more designs and keep one bare tumbler as the comparison.

setup.art: A kitchen thermometer standing in one of the tumblers and a clock beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Read each temperature at the start.

setup.art: A bar graph with one bar for each design showing how many degrees it lost in two hours.
setup.caption: 3. After two hours, draw how many degrees each one lost.

flow.do: An adult runs the geyser tap until the water is hand-hot and pours 200 millilitres into each tumbler from one jug. Read each temperature and write it down.
flow.say: Each tumbler starts the same. Which design do you think will keep the water warm the longest? Why?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to pour the warm water. Write the start temperatures.
flow.parent: If your home has no geyser, an adult warms water in a pan and lets it cool until hand-hot. The adult carries it in a jug.

flow.do: Make the usual designs first. Wrap one tumbler in a thick towel. Put another in a box packed round with crumpled newspaper. Put a lid on every tumbler. Leave one tumbler bare on the table.
flow.say: Which of these slow the heat's leaving? How would they do it?
flow.kid: Wrap one tumbler in a towel. Pack another in a box with newspaper. Leave one bare.

ask.q: Why do crumpled newspaper and a thick towel keep a tumbler warm?
good: They trap air, and air passes heat slowly.
They are insulators, so heat leaves slowly.

flow.parent: The bare tumbler is the comparison, so it must stay out in the open air at room temperature, away from a fan.

flow.do: Now make a creative design. Try one of these or your own. Line a basket with foil and stuff it with straw or old cloth. Stand the tumbler on a ring of card inside a bigger pot, with air all round it. Bury it in a bucket of dry rice. Add a layer of foil inside a box to reflect heat back.
flow.say: What is your design trying to slow down? Heat leaving by air, by touching or by infrared?
flow.kid: Make your own design. Say what it slows down.
flow.parent: A straw-packed basket is how people have kept cooked food hot without fire in many places. Air gaps help, because air passes heat slowly. Foil helps against infrared, because it reflects heat as well as light. A tight lid on every design is fair because it stops warm air escaping.

flow.do: Close each design. Write the time. Leave all of them for one hour. Do not open them.
flow.say: Why do you think we must not peek?
flow.kid: Close every design. Write the time.

flow.do: After one hour, read each tumbler quickly through the lid opening and close it again. Write the temperatures. After a second hour, read them again. Work out how many degrees each design lost.
flow.say: Which design lost the fewest degrees? How big is its lead over the bare tumbler?
flow.kid: Read each tumbler. Write the temperatures. Work out how much each lost.
flow.parent: Heat leaves faster when the tumbler is much hotter than the room. So the drop in the first hour is larger than the drop in the second hour, in every design. In a cold room every design loses more.

flow.do: Put the designs in order from the best keeper to the worst. Say what each one did to slow the heat. Write what you would change to make the best design better.
flow.say: What do the best designs have in common?
flow.kid: Put your designs in order. Write what you would change.
flow.think: Would your best design also keep a cold drink cold, and why?

general: Wrap the tumbler in a thick towel, an old sweater or a cushion, so trapped air slows the heat.
Stand the tumbler in a box packed round with crumpled newspaper, and put a lid on it.
Put a tight lid on the tumbler, because warm air leaving takes heat with it.
creative: Line a basket with foil and straw or old cloth, so that foil turns infrared back and straw traps air.
Stand the tumbler on a ring of card inside a bigger pot, with a gap of still air all round it.
Bury the tumbler in a bucket of dry rice, which holds a lot of air between its grains.
challenges.your_turn: Make a design of your own from things at home and test it against the bare tumbler. What slowed the heat most? Is there a design that could keep the water warm for ever, or does heat always find a way out?

challenges.title: A one-bottle water heater: warm a bottle of water with the Sun
challenges.context: This is a design problem. A solar water heater must catch sunlight, turn it into heat and keep the heat in the water. You make a small heater from a bottle and see how warm you can get it in one hour.
challenges.problem: Warm 1 litre of water as much as possible in one hour of direct sun, using a clear plastic bottle and things from home. A plain bottle of water in the Sun is your comparison. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Every design starts with the same amount of tap water at the same temperature.
Use only things from home, such as black paper, black cloth, a black plastic bag, foil, a clear plastic bag, card and a board.
Every design stands in the same sunny spot for the same 60 minutes.
The water is for testing and is not for drinking afterwards. Use it to water plants.
challenges.safety: Never look at the Sun or at the bright spot that foil throws. The bottle, the water and the black paper can get hot enough to burn, so an adult lifts them.

materials.item: 3 clear 1 litre plastic bottles
black paper or black cloth, a black plastic bag
aluminium foil
a clear plastic bag or a clear plastic sheet
a board, a tray or a stiff card to tilt the bottles
a kitchen thermometer
a measuring jug and tap water
a phone or a watch

setup.art: Three plastic bottles of water: one plain, one wrapped in black paper and one wrapped in black paper inside a clear bag.
setup.caption: 1. Make two or more designs and keep one plain bottle.

setup.art: Three bottles lying on foil on a tilted board in the Sun, facing the Sun.
setup.caption: 2. Set the bottles in the Sun on a tilted board, facing it.

setup.art: A thermometer in the neck of one bottle and a clock.
setup.caption: 3. After an hour, read each temperature.

flow.do: Fill each bottle with 1 litre of the same tap water. Read the start temperature and write it. Wrap one bottle in black paper or black cloth from base to shoulder. Leave one bottle plain.
flow.say: Why do we keep one plain bottle in the Sun?
flow.kid: Fill every bottle with the same water. Write the start temperature. Wrap one bottle in black.
flow.parent: Choose a day with direct sun. If the day is cloudy, wait for a sunny day and do the other parts of this lesson. The clear bottle lets sunlight in, the black wrap absorbs it and turns it into heat that passes into the water.

flow.do: Make the usual designs. Put the black bottle in a clear bag and tie the top. Stand a bottle on foil. Tilt the board towards the Sun. Lay a bottle on its side, so more of it faces the Sun.
flow.say: Which of these helps bring more light in? Which helps keep the heat in?
flow.kid: Put a black bottle in a clear bag. Stand a bottle on foil. Tilt the board towards the Sun.

ask.q: Which design do you think will warm the most, and why?
good: The black bottle in the clear bag, because it absorbs light and keeps the heat in.
The one on foil, because it gets extra light.

flow.parent: A clear bag traps still air round the bottle, like the cover of the Sun Box. Check the aim by looking at the board's shadow, not at the Sun.

flow.do: Make a creative design. Try one of these or your own. Fill a thin black plastic bag with water and lay it flat under a clear sheet. Make a coil of black hose and fill it. Stand two black bottles side by side on foil with a clear sheet over both.
flow.say: Why might a thin flat bag of water warm faster than a tall bottle?
flow.kid: Make a design of your own. Say how it catches light and keeps heat.
flow.parent: A thin layer of water has more surface facing the Sun for each litre of water, so it warms faster than a deep bottle. A black plastic bag may leak, so keep it on a tray. A black hose only needs a bucket for the cold end and a jug for the warm end.

flow.do: Set all of the designs in the same sunny spot. Write the time. Leave them for 60 minutes. Do not move them.
flow.say: What do you think the plain bottle will read?
flow.kid: Set all designs in the Sun. Write the time.
flow.wait: Leave the designs in the Sun for 60 minutes

flow.do: After an hour, an adult lifts each bottle and reads its temperature. Write each one and the rise from the start.
flow.say: Which design rose the most? Which rose the least?
flow.kid: A grown-up reads each bottle. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: Expect the plain bottle to rise a few degrees. Expect the best black and bagged bottle to rise about 8 to 15 degrees in a clear noon hour. A cloudy hour gives much less.

flow.do: Put the designs in order from the warmest to the coolest. Say what each one did to catch sunlight and what it did to keep heat in. Write one change that would make the best one better.
flow.say: What would you add to turn your best design into a real solar water heater?
flow.kid: Put the designs in order. Write one change.
flow.think: Where would you put a tank, and why would the tank need to be above the bottles?

general: Wrap the bottle in black paper or cloth, so it absorbs sunlight and turns it into heat.
Put the black bottle in a clear bag, so a layer of still air slows the heat's leaving.
Stand the bottle on foil and tilt the board towards the Sun, so more light reaches it.
creative: Fill a thin black plastic bag and lay it flat, so more of the water faces the Sun at once.
Make a coil of black hose and fill it, so a long thin stream of water absorbs sunlight.
Stand two black bottles on foil under a clear sheet, so reflected light and held-in air both help.
challenges.your_turn: Build your own heater and test it against the plain bottle. Which part added the most degrees? Could your design heat water all day, or does it have a top temperature?

games.title: The Sun Box game: build a box that keeps the most heat in six rounds
games.context: This is a card game in which each player builds a Sun Box and tries to end with the most heat inside it. Heat comes in from the Sun, leaks out, and the box parts you play change both.

setup.art: A table with 12 Sun cards face down in one pile and 20 box cards face down in another pile, and a hand-drawn ladder numbered 0 to 30 for each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards. Draw a heat ladder from 0 to 30 for each player.

setup.art: Two players each holding four box cards, with a Sun card turned face up between them.
setup.caption: 2. Deal four box cards to each player. Turn over a Sun card.

setup.art: A player's box cards laid out in front of them with a pebble on the heat ladder at 6.
setup.caption: 3. Box parts stay in front of you. Move a pebble up or down your ladder.

printables.title: 12 Sun cards
items: Thin cloud over the Sun. Sunlight 1.
Thin cloud over the Sun. Sunlight 1.

printables.title: 8 event cards
items: Wind blows. Play on everyone. Every box with no Clear lid leaks 2 more heat this round.
Wind blows. Play on everyone. Every box with no Clear lid leaks 2 more heat this round.
A cloud passes. Play on one player. Their Sunlight number is 1 less this round, never below 0.
Someone lifts a lid to peek. Play on one player. They lose 4 heat at once.
Turn the box to face the Sun. Play on yourself. Your In is 1 more this round.
Turn the box to face the Sun. Play on yourself. Your In is 1 more this round.
A tree shadow falls on a box. Play on one player. Their Black lining, Black pot and Foil flap add nothing this round.
A gap opens in the seal. Play on one player with a Clear lid. Their Clear lid protects 0 this round.

printables.title: Heat ladder, to draw by hand for each player
items: Draw a tall ladder of 31 boxes on a sheet and number the boxes from 0 at the bottom to 30 at the top.
Mark the box numbered 15 with the words 'rice is cooked'.
Use a pebble, a coin or a bit of paper as your heat marker, and start it on the box numbered 0.

rules: Each player has a box, a heat ladder and a marker that starts on 0. Heat on the ladder is how much heat is inside your box.
Shuffle the 12 Sun cards face down. Shuffle the 12 box part cards and the 8 event cards together as one box pile. Deal 4 box cards to each player.
The game lasts 6 rounds. Each round starts when you turn over one Sun card. Its number is the sunlight for everyone this round.

Then each player in turn plays one box card or passes. A part card goes face up in front of you and stays until the end. An event card works at once, only for this round, and then goes to the discard pile.
Then every player draws one box card. Nobody holds more than 5 cards.
Now each player works out their own sum. In is the Sun card's number, plus 1 for each In part you have. The In parts add nothing if the Sun card says 0 or 1.

Out is 1, plus 1 for every 4 heat already on your ladder. So 0 to 3 heat adds nothing, 4 to 7 adds 1 and 8 to 11 adds 2. Then take away the Protect on your parts. Out is never less than 1, because no box is perfect.
Move your marker up by In and down by Out. It never goes below 0. Say the sum aloud, for example: In is 4, Out is 2, so my heat goes up by 2.
After round 6 the player with the most heat wins. Players with the same heat share the win. If you reach 15, your rice is cooked.
If the box pile runs out, shuffle the discard pile and use it. Playing alone, build two boxes, A and B, and take turns for them. Try to bring one box to 15 or more.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and shuffle them. Draw a heat ladder from 0 to 30 for each player. Read the three kinds of card together: Sun, part and event.
flow.say: Every round the Sun gives heat and the box leaks heat. Your parts change how much comes in and how much goes out.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Draw a heat ladder from 0 to 30. Shuffle.
flow.parent: Cutting is for the grown-up if the child is under 8. Keep the cards in an envelope after the game for next time.

flow.do: Play round 1 slowly. Turn over a Sun card. Each player plays a card or passes, draws one and works out their sum aloud. Move the markers.
flow.say: In is what comes in. Out is what leaks out. If In is bigger than Out, heat goes up. Which is bigger for you?
flow.kid: Play round 1. Say your In and your Out. Move your marker.
flow.parent: Check each player's sum on the first round. The Out rule is the hardest part: 1, plus 1 for every 4 heat on the ladder, minus Protect, never below 1.

flow.do: Play rounds 2 to 6. Before you play a card, say what job it does: bringing more light in, or slowing the heat's leaving.
flow.say: A Clear lid does one of the two jobs. Which one? Does the foil flap do the same job?
flow.kid: Play rounds 2 to 6. Say each card's job before you play it.

ask.q: When does a box stop getting hotter?
good: When the heat leaving equals the heat coming in.
When Out catches up with In.

flow.parent: Notice when a player's heat stops going up. At that moment, In and Out are equal. That is why the water in an open tumbler stops getting hotter while the Sun still shines.

flow.do: Count the heat on each ladder. Say who won and what parts the winner played. Talk about which part you would keep if you could keep only one.
flow.say: Was a Clear lid worth more than a Foil flap? Could someone defend the other answer?
flow.kid: Say who won. Say which part you would keep.
flow.think: Why can a box never stop heat leaving altogether?

worksheets.title: Sunlight, black and shiny, and the jobs of a box cooker (core)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks three things. You know how sunlight turns into heat. You know which surfaces take it in. You know what each part of a box cooker does.

items.p: Which of these uses sunlight directly, with no machine?
items.why: Drying lets the Sun's energy send the water away as vapour, with no machine. A fan and a mixer use electricity, and a stove burns gas. If you chose one of those, look for the job that needs only open sky.

items.p: A small LED bulb uses about 10 watts. About ____ of them use as much as 1,000 watts.
items.why: 1,000 ÷ 10 = 100. This is how many bulbs one square metre of noon sunlight could run, if all of it could be used.

items.p: Sunlight turns into heat only in the places where something absorbs it.
items.why: True. Light that is reflected goes on as light and warms nothing at that spot. Light that is absorbed turns into heat.

items.p: Match each part of a box cooker to its job.
pairs: Black paper
Absorbs light and turns it into heat
Foil flap
Reflects extra light into the box
Clear cover
Lets light in and holds warm air in
Newspaper packing
Slows heat passing out through the sides
items.a: as given
items.why: Each part does one job. Black takes light in, foil sends more light in, the cover holds air in and packing slows the leaving heat.

items.p: Sort each thing by what it does to most sunlight.
items.a: as given
items.why: Dark, dull surfaces take light in. Pale and shiny surfaces send it away.

items.p: Put the journey of the energy in a solar cooker in order, first to last.
a: Hydrogen joins into helium in the Sun's centre
Light crosses space to the Earth
The black pot absorbs the light
items.why: Energy starts in the Sun's centre, crosses space as light, and turns into heat only where something absorbs it.

items.p: A friend says the foil flap makes heat. What would you say, and how could you test it?
items.a: A strong answer says foil reflects light and makes no heat of its own. It sends more light into the box. A test uses two matching boxes side by side in the same sun, one with a foil flap and one without. Then compare the temperatures.
items.why: A fair answer changes one thing, the flap, and keeps everything else the same.

items.p: About half of the Sun's energy at the ground arrives as a light our eyes cannot see. Which light is it?
items.why: Infrared is the light we feel as warmth. Ultraviolet is also unseen, but it carries much less of the energy at the ground.

items.p: Draw a box cooker from the side. Show where light comes in, where the foil sends it and where heat is held.
items.a: A box with a clear cover on top and a foil flap tilted over it. Arrows of sunlight go in and bounce off the flap. The lining inside is black, with a tumbler in the middle. A label shows warm air held under the cover.
items.why: A drawing shows whether you know how the parts work together: light in, light bounced in and heat held in.

items.p: A shiny silver kettle gets hotter than a matt black kettle of the same size in the same noon sunlight.
items.why: False. The silver kettle reflects most of the light. The black one absorbs most of it, so it gets hotter.

items.p: A rooftop panel is 3 square metres. About how many watts of noon sunlight fall on it?
items.why: 3 × 1,000 = 3,000 watts. A bigger area catches more watts.

items.p: Is a solar cooker a good answer for a family kitchen?

views.who: A health worker in a village (an imagined view)
views.says: Smoke from wood and dung fires harms lungs. A solar cooker makes none, so it protects the cook and the children nearby.

views.who: A mother who cooks after dark (an imagined view)
views.says: My family eats at eight in the evening. A solar cooker works at noon and cannot make rotis, so it does not fit how we cook.

items.ask: Which would matter more to your family, and what would you want to change about the cooker?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer names a real need, such as clean air or cooking after dark. It also names a change, such as keeping the food warm in a box until evening.
items.why: Both views are true for some families. A good design listens to both.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Drying chillies, a solar lantern charging, a window letting in daylight, a gas stove.
items.a: The gas stove. The other three use sunlight that arrives today. A gas stove burns a fuel, and needs no sunlight today.
items.why: The fuel did store sunlight long ago, but the stove does not use the Sun's light that is falling today.

items.p: Wet clothes dry faster in the Sun than in the shade. What does sunlight give the water?
items.why: The Sun's energy lets water leave the cloth as vapour. A cold breeze would not warm the water, and the Sun adds no water.

items.p: A solar cell is a thin slice of ____, a material made from quartz sand.
items.why: Most solar cells are made of silicon.

items.p: Name three ways your family uses the Sun's heat or light on an ordinary day. What changes in a cloudy week?
items.a: Three real examples, such as drying clothes, daylight in a room and warm water from a rooftop heater. A strong answer says what is slower or missing on a cloudy week, such as clothes taking longer to dry or lamps staying on.
items.why: A good answer is specific to the family's day.

worksheets.title: Heat coming in, heat leaving, and the water heater (stretch)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks that you can compare the heat coming in with the heat leaving. It also checks that you understand the solar water heater and the solar cell.

items.p: A bucket fills while its drain is open, and the level stops rising. What does this match in a sunlit tumbler?
opts: Heat leaves as fast as it comes in
The water is full of heat
items.why: The level stops when water leaves as fast as it enters. A tumbler's temperature stops when heat leaves as fast as sunlight brings it in.

items.p: Warm water is a little ____ than the same amount of cold water, so it rises.
items.why: Warm water spreads out a little, so a litre of it weighs slightly less than a litre of cold water.

items.p: With its tank lower than its tubes, a heater would still move warm water up with no pump.
items.why: False. Warm water rises, so it needs the tank above the tubes. A tank lower down would have nothing to push the warm water to it.

items.p: You lift the lid of a hot box for ten seconds and the temperature drops at once. What left?
items.why: The warm air carried its heat away. This is why the cover's main job is holding the warm air in.

items.p: Put the journey of the water in a solar water heater in order, first to last.
a: Black tubes absorb light and warm the water
Warm water, now lighter, rises into the tank
Cold water from the tank sinks down into the tubes
The wrapped tank keeps the water hot until morning
items.why: The Sun warms the tube water, and the warm water rises into the tank. Cold water takes its place, and the wrapped tank stores the heat.

items.p: Match each hot thing to the reason it is hot.
pairs: A parked car with its windows shut
Sunlight comes in and warm air cannot get out
A black tar road
It absorbs nearly all the light
The pot of a dish cooker
A mirror brings the light of a wide area to it
The tank of a solar water heater
It is wrapped in an insulator
items.a: as given
items.why: Each hot thing either takes in a lot of light, collects light from a wide area or slows the heat's leaving.

items.p: Sort each part by its job in a hot box.
items: tilting the box towards the Sun
items.a: as given
items.why: A hot box either gets more light or loses heat more slowly. Both make the water hotter.

items.p: The Sun Box test changed the cover, the black paper and the foil at once. What can it not tell us?
items.a: It cannot tell us which part mattered most. To find out, change one part at a time. Keep a twin box beside it and compare the rise each time.
items.why: A test that changes many things at once cannot show which one did the work.

items.p: A box has a clear cover of 0.1 square metre. About how many watts of noon sunlight fall on it?
items.why: 0.1 × 1,000 = 100 watts. A small catching area catches few watts.

items.p: A solar street lamp lights up at night. Where does the night's energy come from?
opts: The day's sunlight, stored in a battery
items.why: The panel works by day and fills a battery. The battery lights the lamp after dark.

items.p: Solar cells work in space, where there is no air.
items.why: True. Sunlight crosses empty space, and a cell needs only light. Vanguard 1 ran on solar cells in 1958.

items.p: Draw a solar water heater. Show the tubes, the tank and arrows for the way warm water moves.
items.a: Slanted black tubes under glass, with a wrapped tank above them. An arrow goes up from the warm tubes to the tank. A second arrow goes down from the cooler bottom of the tank into the tubes.
items.why: The drawing should show the tank above the tubes and the water going round in a loop.

items.p: Should big solar parks be built on desert grazing land?

views.who: A herder in Rajasthan (an imagined view)
views.says: This grazing land feeds our animals. If panels cover it, we lose our living.
Deserts get strong sun and have few people. Solar power cuts smoke and helps the whole country.
Great Indian bustards live there and die on power lines. Lines must go underground or the parks must move.

items.ask: What would you want to know before you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer asks who uses the land, how many birds live there and whether roofs could do the job instead.
items.why: No single view is wrong. Each describes a real cost or a real gain.

items.p: A solar cell is dark blue or black. What does the colour tell you?
opts: It absorbs light and reflects little
items.why: A dark surface absorbs most light. A solar cell needs to absorb light so photons can free its electrons.

items.p: Which would suit a school kitchen better, a dish cooker or a box cooker? Which would suit one family? Say why.
items.a: A strong answer says a dish cooker gets very hot and cooks large amounts quickly but needs turning. A box cooker is cheap, needs less turning and suits one family's dal and rice. Either answer is fine if the reason is clear.
items.why: The best design depends on how many people eat, when they eat and what they cook.

items.p: Which is the odd one out? A solar cooker, a solar water heater, a solar cell, a solar dryer.
items.a: The solar cell. It turns light straight into electricity. The others use the Sun's heat.
items.why: A cell needs no heating step. In fact, it works better when it stays cool.

worksheets.title: Where the energy goes, and what science cannot yet say (challenge)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks you to think about where energy goes, what a machine really does, and what nobody can yet say about energy.

items.p: A panel turns 20 of every 100 parts of sunlight into electricity. Where do most of the other 80 parts go?
opts: Mostly into heat in the panel, and some is reflected
items.why: Energy is not lost. It turns into heat, or the light bounces away. Thinking the rest vanishes forgets that the total stays the same.

items.p: If a box had a perfect lid and perfect walls, its water would heat without any limit.
items.why: False. A perfect box does not exist, and the hotter the water gets, the faster it sends out heat as infrared. The temperature levels off.

items.p: A tumbler gets hotter while heat comes in ____ than it leaves.
items.why: When heat in is bigger than heat out, the temperature rises. When they are equal, it stays the same.

items.p: Which sentence is the most accurate?
opts: The cooker holds the Sun's heat and slows its leaving
The cooker makes the Sun hotter
items.why: A cooker adds no energy. It lets sunlight in and slows the heat's leaving, so the heat builds up.

items.p: Feynman wrote that physics today has no knowledge of what energy is. Yet engineers use energy sums. How can both be true?
items.a: Energy is a number that physicists work out for light, heat and movement, and the total stays the same. The sums predict what happens and work, even though nobody can say what energy finally is. A strong answer gives an example of a sum that works.
items.why: Science can use an idea well and still not know its deepest meaning. Saying so is honest.

items.p: Put these in order from the least to the most noon sunlight falling on them.
items.why: Watts grow with the area. They are 500, 1,000 and 2,000 for the first three, and tens of crores for the park.

items.p: Without gases in the air, Earth's average would be about 18 degrees below zero. What does this share with the Sun Box?
opts: Both slow the leaving of heat
items.why: Gases such as water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb some of the infrared that leaves the Earth, and so slow its leaving. The box does the same with its cover.

items.p: Draw both tumblers' temperatures in the Sun Box test, start to finish. Show where each line levels off.
items.a: Both lines start at the same temperature. The open tumbler's line rises a little and flattens early at a lower temperature. The box tumbler's line rises more and flattens later at a higher one.
items.why: Both lines flatten when the heat leaving equals the heat coming in. The box's line flattens higher because its heat leaves more slowly.

items.p: Is energy a real thing, or only a number that scientists calculate?

views.says: In physics today we have no knowledge of what energy is. We have a number that does not change when things change.
The number predicts everything we build, from panels to cookers. Something that predicts so well must be as real as a stone.

items.ask: What would you want to test, to decide between these views?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer accepts that the number is solid and useful, and says that whether it is a thing is still open.
items.why: Scientists agree on what the number does. They do not agree on what it is.

items.p: A panel gives 400 watts. Heat cuts its output by 15 of every 100. About how many watts does it give then?
items.why: 15 of every 100 of 400 is 60. 400 − 60 = 340 watts.

items.p: A family cooks at 8 in the evening. Their cooker works at noon. Which change helps most?
opts: Keep the cooked food hot in a packed, insulated container
items.why: Packed straw or cloth slows the heat's leaving for hours. The other changes bring less light in or let heat out.

items.p: Write one question about sunlight or energy that nobody can answer yet. Say how someone might start to find out.
items.a: Any real open question, such as what energy is, or how the Sun's corona is hotter than its surface. A strong answer names a first step, such as a measurement or a test.
items.why: A good question can be tested or compared, even if nobody knows the answer yet.

items.p: Match each way heat leaves a tumbler to a thing you can see or feel.
pairs: Moving air carries it off
Wind blowing over a tumbler
It is sent out as invisible infrared
A warm tumbler warms your hand from a distance
It passes into what the tumbler touches
A tumbler on a cold steel table
Trapped air slows all of these
A tumbler packed in crumpled paper
items.a: as given
items.why: Heat leaves by moving air, by infrared and by touch. Trapped air slows all three.

items.p: A solar panel gets more electricity from the Sun's heat than from its light.
items.why: False. A panel uses the light. Heat harms it, which is why a hot panel gives less.

items.p: Sort each claim by how firmly we know it.
items: The Sun's energy comes from hydrogen joining into helium
A hot panel gives less electricity than a cool one
Solar cookers are a good answer to cooking smoke
Big solar parks should use desert grazing land
A clear cover mostly stops warm air leaving
items.a: as given
items.why: Some claims are measured many times. Others depend on how people cook, who owns land and what we value.

items.p: Your family lives where the sky is cloudy for months. How could you still use the Sun, and what would you add?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer uses sunny hours with a heat store or a battery. It says what else is needed, such as another power source for cloudy weeks.
items.why: No single method fits every place. Good designs fit the place and the weather.

quiz.p: A rooftop panel is 2 square metres. About how many watts of noon sunlight land on it?
quiz.why: 1,000 watts fall on each square metre, and the panel covers 2, so 2 × 1,000 = 2,000. Choosing 1,000 counts one square metre only. Multiply by the area.

quiz.p: A black scooter seat is too hot to sit on, though nothing touched it. What made it hot?
opts: Sunlight that the seat absorbed turned into heat
The seat made its own heat
Hot air from under the seat rose into it
quiz.why: Light that a dark surface absorbs turns into heat in that surface. The seat has no flame or wire and makes no energy of its own.

quiz.p: A friend colours the inside of a box cooker white. What happens to the heat inside?
opts: It rises, because white is bright
It is lower, because white sends light away
quiz.why: White reflects much of the light, so less is absorbed and less turns into heat. Black is the colour that absorbs.

quiz.p: Which part of a box cooker mostly stops warm air from blowing away?
quiz.why: The clear cover lets light in and holds the warm air in. The foil flap sends more light in, and the black lining absorbs light.

quiz.p: In the Sun Box test, the box adds no heat. Why is its water hotter?
opts: Heat leaves the water in the box more slowly
More air reaches the box water
quiz.why: The box slows the heat's leaving. Both tumblers get the same sunlight, but the box tumbler loses heat more slowly. Foil sends light in and makes no heat.

quiz.p: A black tumbler in open sun stops at 45 degrees Celsius while the Sun still shines. Why?
opts: Heat leaves as fast as sunlight brings it in
The water is full of heat
quiz.why: As the tumbler warms, it loses heat faster. At 45 degrees the heat leaving equals the heat arriving, so the temperature stays steady.

quiz.p: You want to test only the clear cover. Which test is fair?
opts: Two matching boxes side by side, one with a cover and one without
One box with a cover on Monday and without on Tuesday
A large box with a cover against a small box without
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing and keeps the Sun the same. Different days or different boxes change more than one thing.

quiz.p: Why is the tank of a solar water heater above its tubes?
opts: Warmed water rises, so it flows up into the tank
A heavy tank needs to be high
Warm water is heavier and sinks into the tank
quiz.why: Warm water is a little lighter, so cold water pushes it up and it moves into the tank with no pump. Warm water sinking is the wrong way round.

quiz.p: Many solar heater tubes have two glass walls with no air between them. What does this do?
opts: Slows heat leaking out, like a flask
quiz.why: With no air between the walls, very little heat can pass through. The water stays hot. The tubes are made to hold heat, not to cool.

quiz.p: A rooftop panel gives less electricity on a hot afternoon than on a cold clear day. Why?
opts: Hot silicon pushes its electrons less strongly
A hot day has less sunlight
quiz.why: A solar cell uses light, not heat. Warm silicon gives a smaller push to the freed electrons, so the panel gives less electricity.

opts: A solar cell heats water to make electricity
A solar cooker turns light into electricity
A solar cell turns light into electricity without heating anything first
Both a cooker and a cell need a mirror
quiz.why: A solar cell frees electrons with light and needs no heating step. A cooker turns light into heat. Neither needs a mirror, though a flap helps a cooker.

quiz.p: A solar cooker is slow and fails in the monsoon. What is the fairest conclusion?
opts: They suit some kitchens and need better design for others
Families who stopped using them were wrong
quiz.why: People disagree about solar cookers. They fit some families well and others poorly, so the honest answer names who they suit and what to improve.

quiz.p: Which question about energy has no agreed answer yet?
opts: How many watts fall on a square metre at noon?
quiz.why: Physicists calculate energy and trust the sums. They have no final answer to what it is. The other questions have been measured.

maths.problem: A tray on a terrace is 0.5 metre long and 0.4 metre wide. At noon about 1,000 watts of sunlight fall on each square metre. How many watts fall on the tray?
maths.explain: The tray's area is 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2 square metres. Then 0.2 × 1,000 = 200 watts. A tray one fifth of a square metre catches one fifth of 1,000 watts.
maths.context: This problem works out how many watts of sunlight a small flat thing catches, using its area.
maths.why_maths: Every way of using the Sun starts with area times watts for each square metre. A bigger catching area catches more watts.

maths.problem: A tumbler holds 150 grams of water. It takes roughly 630 joules to warm it by 1 degree Celsius. How many joules does it take to warm it by 30 degrees? A heater of 100 watts gives 100 joules each second. How many seconds would it need if none of the heat leaked out?
maths.explain: 630 × 30 = 18,900 joules. At 100 joules each second, 18,900 ÷ 100 = 189 seconds, about 3 minutes. The real Sun Box takes about 60 minutes, nearly 20 times longer. Most of the light misses the tumbler, and much of the heat leaks out.
maths.context: This problem works out the least time a perfect heater would need to warm a tumbler of water. Then it compares that with the real test.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the perfect sum with the real result shows how much heat is lost. This is the sum an engineer does to judge a design.

maths.problem: A panel of 2 square metres sits in noon sun of 1,000 watts on each square metre. It turns 20 of every 100 parts into electricity. How many watts of electricity does it give? How many 10-watt LED bulbs could it run?
maths.explain: The sunlight on the panel is 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 watts. Then 20 of every 100 parts of 2,000 is 2,000 × 20 ÷ 100 = 400 watts. 400 ÷ 10 = 40 bulbs.
maths.context: This problem finds how much electricity a panel gives from the sunlight that lands on it.
maths.why_maths: Parts in a hundred, which are percentages, tell us how much of the Sun's energy a machine can use. This is how a panel is sized for a house.

maths.problem: These are imagined readings from a box tumbler. At 0, 15, 30, 45 and 60 minutes it read 28, 38, 47, 54 and 59 degrees Celsius. Find the rise in each 15 minutes. What do the rises tell you about heat coming in and heat leaving?
maths.answer: 10, 9, 7 and 5 degrees. The rises shrink, so the heat leaving grows as the water gets hotter, and it is getting closer to the heat coming in.
maths.explain: 38 − 28 = 10, 47 − 38 = 9, 54 − 47 = 7 and 59 − 54 = 5. A hotter tumbler loses heat faster, so less of the arriving heat is left to raise the temperature each time. The graph bends and flattens.
maths.context: This problem reads a line of readings from a tumbler in a box and explains why the line bends.
maths.why_maths: A graph that flattens shows two flows closing in on each other. Reading the rises tells us this without any more measuring.

maths.problem: Light travels about 3 lakh kilometres each second. The Sun is about 15 crore kilometres away. How many seconds does sunlight take to reach the Earth? How many minutes is that?
maths.explain: 15 crore is 15,00,00,000 and 3 lakh is 3,00,000. 15,00,00,000 ÷ 3,00,000 = 500 seconds. 500 ÷ 60 is about 8 minutes and 20 seconds.
maths.context: This problem uses the distance to the Sun and the speed of light to find how long sunlight takes to arrive.
maths.why_maths: Distance divided by speed gives the time. Working with lakh and crore shows how large the Sun's distance is.

maths.problem: The Earth catches less than 1 part of every 200 crore of the Sun's light. Write 200 crore in figures. How many zeros does it have after the 2?
maths.explain: 1 crore is 1,00,00,000. 200 crore is 200 × 1,00,00,000 = 2,00,00,00,000. That is a 2 followed by 9 zeros, or 2 thousand million.
maths.context: This problem writes the Earth's small share of the Sun's light as a number in figures.
maths.why_maths: Big numbers such as crore are easy to say and hard to picture. Writing them in figures shows how little of the Sun's light the Earth catches.

maths.problem: These are imagined readings. In the Sun Box test the open tumbler rose 14 degrees and the box tumbler rose 34 degrees. How many degrees more did the box tumbler rise? About how many times bigger was its rise?
maths.explain: 34 − 14 = 20 degrees. 34 ÷ 14 is about 2.4. The box's rise was a little more than twice the open tumbler's rise.
maths.context: This problem compares the two rises from a Sun Box test, as a difference and as a ratio.
maths.why_maths: A difference says how much more, and a ratio says how many times more. Scientists often give both to compare two results fairly.

jokes.j: What did the black tumbler say to the white tumbler in the Sun?
jokes.a: 'You are so cool. I am just taking it all in.'

jokes.j: What does a solar street lamp eat for a midnight snack?
jokes.a: Leftovers from the battery. The Sun's dinner was at noon.

jokes.j: Why does a solar cooker never win a race?
jokes.a: It is great at slow cooking.

jokes.j: Why did the Sun not go to college?
Why did the lizard refuse to leave the sunny wall?
jokes.a: He was basking in his own glory.

jokes.j: What did one solar cell say to the other?
Why did the thermometer join the Sun Box club?
jokes.a: It wanted to earn a few more degrees.

jokes.j: Why was the foil flap invited to every Sun Box party?
jokes.a: It always knew how to bring the light.

jokes.j: What did one hydrogen atom say to another in the middle of the Sun?
jokes.a: 'Let's join together and make something bright.'

warmup.q: Which light carries about half of the Sun's energy at the ground, and we cannot see it?
Which takes in more sunlight, matt black or white?
warmup.a: Matt black. White reflects much of it.
How fast energy arrives or is used.

warmup.q: Which machine turns light straight into electricity: a solar cooker or a solar cell?
Does a shiny foil flap make heat or send in more light?
warmup.a: It sends in more light. It makes no heat.

warmup.q: Where does a solar water heater keep its hot water?
warmup.a: In a wrapped tank above the tubes.

warmup.q: Does a solar panel work better on a hot day or a cold clear day?
warmup.a: A cold clear day. Heat lowers its output.

quiz: Sunlight crosses space to the Earth in about eight minutes.
The Sun is about 15 crore kilometres away, and light covers that distance in about 8 minutes.
A white surface absorbs more sunlight than a black one.
Black absorbs nearly all the light that lands on it. White reflects much of it away.
Part of sunlight is light that our eyes cannot see.
Infrared and ultraviolet are in sunlight. Infrared carries about half of the energy that reaches the ground.
A solar cell needs to be hot to work well.
A hot cell gives less electricity than a cool one in the same light.
A clear lid helps a hot box mostly by keeping warm air from escaping.
Robert Wood showed in 1909 that glass and rock salt lids gave nearly the same heat.
A solar panel gives electricity at night.
No light falls on the panel at night. A battery can store the day's electricity for the night.
Warm water is a little lighter than the same amount of cold water.
This is why warm water rises in a solar water heater.
The Sun makes its energy by burning wood.
In the Sun's centre, hydrogen joins to make helium, and that gives out energy.
Foil reflects light, so it can send extra sunlight into a box.
Foil is shiny, so most of the light that lands on it bounces away in a new direction.
A solar cooker makes heat that the Sun does not provide.
It only catches the Sun's energy and slows the heat's leaving.
odd: Foil reflects most sunlight. The other three absorb it.
A watt measures how fast energy flows. The others measure size.
A battery stores electricity. The others work with the light itself.
The others are living beings that warm themselves in the Sun.
The other three are kinds of light in sunlight. Sound is not light.

applications: Hostels, hospitals and homes in cities such as Bengaluru, Pune and Shimla heat bathing water with solar water heaters on the roof. Find the tank and the glass tubes on a roof near you.
Street lamps and lanterns with a small panel on top fill a battery by day and shine at night. Look at one at dusk and see when it switches on.
At Shirdi in Maharashtra, rows of large dish cookers on a kitchen roof make steam. The steam cooks meals for tens of thousands of people a day.
Women trained at Barefoot College in Tilonia, Rajasthan, build and mend solar cookers and solar lights for their own villages.
At the salt pans of Thoothukudi and Kutch, the Sun dries sea water to leave salt. Dried chillies, tamarind and fish are also kept for months by sun-drying.
Many satellites from India run on solar cells. In a picture of a satellite, find the long flat wings. Those are its solar panels.
A white painted terrace in Chennai or Ahmedabad reflects much sunlight and keeps the rooms below cooler. Find a white roof and a dark roof near you and touch the walls beneath them.
A closed car in the Sun gets much hotter than the outside air. Sunlight comes in through the glass and the warm air cannot leave. No child or animal is ever left in a shut car.
ask_kids: Where in our home does the Sun land at noon? Where does it land in the evening?
Which of the things we wear or use is black? How does it feel after an hour in the Sun?
If you could have just one solar machine for our home, would it be a cooker, a heater or a cell? Why?
What does a lizard know about the Sun that we have to learn from books?
The box added no heat, yet its water was hotter. What does that make you think about the word 'make'?
Scientists have no agreed definition of life, only working ones. A lizard warms on a wall and a leaf builds sugar from light. Are they doing the same thing as a solar panel, or something different?

buy.plan: Instead, use the touch test, where an adult dips a fingertip for one second and you write cool, warm, hot or too hot.

buy.why: The clear cover of the Sun Box. A clear file cover or an overhead projector sheet from a stationery shop costs about ₹5 to ₹20.
buy.plan: Instead, use the lid of a clear sweet box. Or use the glass of an old photo frame with its edges taped, handled by an adult.

buy.why: To line the box, wrap the tumblers and cover the bottles. About ₹10 a sheet at any stationery shop.

buy.why: To see a solar cell at work. A solar calculator costs about ₹150 to ₹250 and a small solar fan kit about ₹150 to ₹400.
